summary:
Kastamonu province stands under the national framework of Turkey: the criminal law, health regulation, identity-document rules and detention practice that determine what a trans visitor faces are set at national level and apply in Kastamonu as elsewhere. No statute, enforcement action, incident or court decision specific to Kastamonu appears in the sources assembled for this record.

On 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch reported a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; health professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

The draft had not been reported as passed, but the prohibitions it contains are already being applied. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in streets, shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not been passed even as it was being applied to them.

Foreign nationals must carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. For a trans visitor in Kastamonu, every checkpoint stop is an occasion on which a passport gender marker is compared against presentation. That is the most direct outing risk in the province.

Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people has become explicit state policy rather than residual prejudice: "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases against 11 of its members, and artistic events cancelled or banned. The review records roughly 313 violations in the year, about 2.5 times the previous total, with 299 detention decisions — 256 through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — 89 torture or ill-treatment violations against 51 the prior year, six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings in which trans people were the most affected, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

Under that framing the Erdoğan government has repeatedly invoked protection of "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies. A visitor considering public visibility in Kastamonu should read that as the ceiling on assembly tolerance nationwide.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Residents of Kastamonu also live under the national policy measures recorded in 2025: "Year of the Family" directives to public institutions, closure of an LGBTI+ association with criminal cases against 11 members, and cancellation or banning of artistic and broadcast events.
outOfScopeNotes:
No statute, incident, police action or court case specific to Kastamonu appears in the surviving sources for this record; the documents behind this profile describe the national framework and examples drawn from other provinces. Whether Kastamonu police conduct identity-document checks of the kind recorded in Istanbul, and how often, is unresolved and not sourced here.

The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of 29 October 2025 and had not been reported as enacted. Whether it has since been passed, amended or withdrawn is unresolved in the sources available; the enforcement described above rests on administrative practice and police stops rather than on a statute in force.

The violation totals, detention counts and killing figures come from NGO monitoring — Kaos GL, Human Rights Watch, the Truth Justice Memory Center — rather than official statistics, and no official count of anti-trans incidents has been located for comparison. Hate-crime charging outcomes in the 2025 killings, including whether any suspect was prosecuted under an aggravating-provision framework, are not sourced here.

The Kayseri circular and the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation are reported through secondary coverage; the operative text of the regulation and whether Kastamonu facilities apply it as described are unresolved.
